Address retained by Jeedom = 127.0.0.1 or the Jeedom machine's: a local tunnel or proxy, to make pass the address on; never remove it from the whitelist.
plugins/secaudit/desktop/php/secaudit.ph.Adresse de connexion inconnue (PHP hors: Connection address unknown (PHP not running as an Apache module, sudo refused to www-data, or ss missing): if the phone's IP appears nowhere, it is the previous case; otherwise neither disable nor declare anything before reading the connection address, over SSH (sudo ss -tnp state established right after reloading the page, several times, only the apache2 or httpd lines on an Apache listening port). Before that, close the other apps and other tabs that reach Jeedom and wait 10 s after a test through another access address. Phone's IP only in a header: proxy, whatever ss shows. Otherwise, direct access only if the phone's IP is, on every reading, the only address; a 127.0.0.1 or ::1 line points to a likely local proxy, to confirm in its configuration. Another address may be another visitor's: declare it only if the proxy's configuration confirms it. When in doubt, declare nothing.

plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Informatif. VM : sauvegarder aussi la VM: For information. VM: also back up the VM itself and keep the host up to date (Jeedom's security depends on it). Raspberry Pi: SD cards are fragile, keep Jeedom backups off the card. Docker: only publish the ports you need.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Chaque administrateur active la double a: Each administrator turns on two-factor authentication from their profile (user icon › Profile › Security tab) with a TOTP app. On a standard Jeedom install, www-data has passwordless sudo: a Jeedom administrator is root on the machine.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Supprimer les comptes inutiles : Réglage: Delete unused accounts: Settings › System › Users, delete button.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.API HTTP de Jeedom ouverte à tous: Jeedom HTTP API open to everyone
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Les appels à l'API depuis une adresse ho: API calls from addresses outside the whitelist will be refused: mobile apps on 4G, iOS Shortcuts, IFTTT… First check in Analysis › Logs › api who calls it.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.API JSON-RPC de Jeedom ouverte à tous: Jeedom JSON-RPC API open to everyone
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Réglages › Système › Configuration › Séc: Settings › System › Configuration › Security: 5 to 6 attempts at most, ban for at least 10 minutes.

plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Réglages › Système › Centre de mise à jo: Settings › System › Update center: take a backup, then update.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.En SSH : `sudo apt update && sudo apt up: Over SSH: `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade`. To automate it: `sudo apt install unattended-upgrades` (security updates only by default).
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Fichiers lisibles sans connexion dans da: Files readable without login in data/
In /var/www/html/data/, .js, .css, .html and .txt files are served without authentication (backups, exports…). Move them out of the web root or rename them to .json (blocked by Apache).
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Fichiers recherchés par les robots et se: Files probed by bots and served by Apache
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Chaque chemin demandé par une IP extérie: Every path requested by an outside IP (http.error log) is recorded. If it exists here, the audit requests it locally: a 200 response means anyone can read it. Delete the file, move it out of /var/www/html or deny it in the Apache configuration. A PHP script that was missing when a bot asked for it and is present now is reported too (unless the plugin shipped it before the request, or a Jeedom update installed it afterwards): open it and make sure it is not a backdoor. If in doubt, move it out of /var/www/html rather than deleting it, and find out how it got there. The warning clears after 90 days.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Jeedom croit les en-têtes X-Forwarded-Fo: Jeedom trusts X-Forwarded-For and similar headers: an attacker can pose as a whitelisted IP and dodge banning
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.SSH : connexion root par mot de passe au: SSH: root login with password allowed
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.1) S'il n'y a aucune clé (voir le consta: 1) If there is no key (see the finding): from the computer, `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` then `ssh-copy-id user@jeedom-ip`, and check that a new login no longer asked for the password. 2) Only then, create /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-secaudit.conf with `PasswordAuthentication no` and `KbdInteractiveAuthentication no` (a file in this folder wins over sshd_config: the first value read wins), then `sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh`, and check with `sudo sshd -T | grep -i authentication`. Keep a session open during the test. Every user and machine listed in the finding must have their key, otherwise they lose access. If the "since" date is recent, the journal is wiped at reboot: older logins may have escaped the finding.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.SSH : X11Forwarding activé (inutile sur: SSH: X11Forwarding enabled (useless on a server)
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Dans /etc/ssh/sshd_config : `X11Forwardi: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config: `X11Forwarding no`, then `sudo systemctl reload ssh`.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Apache remoteip sans proxy de confiance: Apache remoteip without a trusted proxy (client IP can be spoofed)
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Z-Wave JS UI (port 8091) ouvert sans aut: Z-Wave JS UI (port 8091) open without authentication or not verifiable
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Services ouverts à tout le réseau local: Services open to the whole local network
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Pour chaque port listé : « répond sans m: For each listed port: "answers without a password" = any device on the network can use it (a Signal container sends messages, for example); "web page served" = open http://jeedom-ip:PORT and see whether a password is asked; "(HTTP code)": other answer, open it the same way; no mention: port not probed (not a known web server) or not HTTP. If only Jeedom uses it, bind it to 127.0.0.1. Container created by Docker management (or by a plugin through it): in the equipment, `ports:` → `"127.0.0.1:PORT:INTERNAL_PORT"` then Recreate; a plugin that reinstalls its dependencies may rewrite it, check again afterwards. Plain Docker: `-p 127.0.0.1:PORT:PORT`. Other service: its listen address in its configuration, or a password. A port that is intended and protected goes into "Accepted ports" in the plugin configuration. Never forward them on your router.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Appels à l'API Jeedom refusés en boucle: Jeedom API calls refused over and over
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Normal sur Jeedom (nécessaire aux plugin: Normal on Jeedom (plugins need it). Consequence: any administrator access to Jeedom means root. Hence two-factor authentication, a restricted API and keeping up to date.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Redirections de ports de la box : à véri: Router port forwarding: check by hand
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Jeedom antérieur à 4.6.2 (protections PH: Jeedom older than 4.6.2 (PHP and Apache protections)
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Mettre Jeedom à jour (Réglages › Système: Update Jeedom (Settings › System › Update center). 4.6.2 hardens PHP against a known vulnerability (session.upload_progress, max_input_nesting_level) and adds them to Apache's security configuration (security.conf).
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Le constat liste les lignes de /var/www/: The finding lists the lines of /var/www/html/install/apache_security (shipped by Jeedom) missing from the active configuration (/etc/apache2/conf-enabled/security.conf, a link to conf-available). If this is not intended: the « Apache sécurisé » (secure Apache) button (Settings › System › Configuration › OS/DB › System administration), or over SSH `sudo cp /var/www/html/install/apache_security /etc/apache2/conf-available/security.conf`, `sudo a2enconf security`, `sudo apache2ctl configtest` then `sudo systemctl reload apache2` (if conf-enabled/security.conf is a real file rather than a link, delete it before `a2enconf`). A personal setting belongs in a separate file in conf-available instead (since 4.5, a Jeedom update rewrites security.conf if it contains jeedom.com).
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Réglages › Système › Configuration › Rés: Settings › System › Configuration › Networks/Security: whitelisted addresses are never banned and can use the APIs in "White IP" mode. Keep only 127.0.0.1 and your local subnet (e.g. 192.168.1.*). Behind a proxy not declared in remoteip (see the “Address diagnosis” (plugin page)), every visitor has the proxy's address: the fix is to declare it in remoteip (remoteip rule), not to touch the whitelist. Behind NAT, every visitor has the gateway's address, often covered by the local subnet: before changing the list, follow the NAT paragraph of the X-Forwarded-For headers rule (narrower entries covering the local machines without the gateway, local network devices going through it, ban risk, rollback over SSH).
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Retire de la liste blanche les entrées p: Removes from the whitelist entries wider than a /24 (10.*, 192.168.*.*, 192.*.1.*, 10.0.0.0/8, *…), unreadable entries (192.168.1.01-…) and any IPv6 network (even your /64; an exact IPv6 address is kept): a Docker container, VPN or second network that relied on them may get banned and will lose API access in White IP mode. The fix also adds 127.0.0.1 and your local subnet: do not apply it if a NAT gateway on that network forwards Internet visitors (it is not declared in remoteip: see the NAT case of the X-Forwarded-For headers rule), nor if a proxy on that network or on the Jeedom machine is not declared in remoteip (every visitor would have its address, or 127.0.0.1): declare the proxy first (see the “Address diagnosis” (plugin page)).
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Mettre un certificat (Let's Encrypt / ce: Install a certificate (Let's Encrypt / certbot) and switch external access to https:// in Settings › System › Configuration › Networks. Redirect port 80 to https. Behind a reverse proxy that handles HTTPS, the certificate and the redirect belong on the proxy, not on Jeedom (otherwise a redirect loop).
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Renouveler : `sudo certbot renew` puis `: Renew it: `sudo certbot renew` then `sudo systemctl reload apache2`. Make sure the certbot timer is active (`systemctl list-timers | grep certbot`) and that port 80 (acme-challenge) is reachable. This test reads Jeedom's own certificate: if a proxy presents its own certificate to visitors, renew that one too.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.`sudo apt install fail2ban`, puis active: `sudo apt install fail2ban`, then enable at least the sshd and apache jails (in /etc/fail2ban/jail.local). Behind a reverse proxy: then check in the Apache logs that the addresses are the visitors' and not the proxy's; otherwise, until the proxy is declared in remoteip, put its address in ignoreip: fail2ban would ban the proxy, and so everyone.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Proxy déclaré devant Jeedom : à vérifier: Proxy declared in front of Jeedom: to be checked from outside
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Le constat liste les proxys déclarés dan: The finding lists the proxies declared in remoteip. secaudit cannot see what sits in front of Jeedom: neither whether this proxy still exists nor what it does with the headers. Check from time to time, from a phone on 4G (no Wi-Fi, no VPN; if Jeedom can only be reached through a VPN, through the VPN, comparing with the phone's VPN address), with the “Address diagnosis” (plugin page): the address seen by Apache and the one retained by Jeedom must be the phone's public IP. Remove from the declaration any address that is no longer a proxy: a declared machine can choose its clients' address. If the proxy passes the address in another header (CF-Connecting-IP…), RemoteIPHeader must name that one. A proxy's address can change (Jeedom DNS, VPN, new machine): run the diagnosis again after a change or a reconnection. Declare the proxies in the global remoteip.conf, at the same level as RemoteIPHeader, not in a single vhost: the other vhosts would believe any client, and secaudit does not read the scope.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.L'interface Z-Wave JS UI donne le contrô: The Z-Wave JS UI interface gives full control of the Z-Wave network (exclusion, reset). Turn on its authentication (Settings › General › Auth, then change the default "zwave" password of the admin account) or, if only Jeedom on this machine uses it, bind it to 127.0.0.1. Never forward this port on your router.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Le constat nomme l'adresse, ses clients: The finding names the address, its clients (plugin) and who owns the refused key. "key of disabled account": often a plugin daemon that kept the key of an admin disabled since then (Homebridge…). Restart that daemon (plugin page › Daemon): it regenerates its configuration with an active admin. "unknown key": regenerated key or misconfigured app, give it a valid key again; if the address is outside, someone is guessing keys. "valid key": the API is in "White IP" mode or the key lacks that right, whitelist the address, unless it is that of a proxy or NAT gateway every visitor goes through (see the “Address diagnosis” (plugin page)). "refusals from the Internet": keys are being tried from outside (several addresses or changing names); open the API to known addresses only (whitelist) and do not forward it on your router. "address attribution not guaranteed": many refusals the log does not tie to any address, read the api log. "forgeable addresses": the X-Forwarded-For headers rule or the remoteip rule is failing, the addresses in the finding may be fake.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.D'abord donner un identifiant et un mot: First give a username and password to every client (Zigbee2MQTT, Z-Wave JS, Jeedom plugins…), otherwise they lose access. Then, in the mosquitto configuration (or the MQTT Manager plugin): `allow_anonymous false` and a password file, and check that the devices still respond. Any anonymous MQTT client can control the Zigbee / Z-Wave devices.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Dans l'interface de la box : seul le 443: In your router's interface, only 443 (and 80 for certificate renewal) should be forwarded to Jeedom (or to the reverse proxy, if there is one). Never 22, 1883, 3306, 8080 or 8091. Once checked, tick "Router port forwarding checked" in the plugin configuration.
plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Réglages › Système › Configuration › API: Settings › System › Configuration › API: set the HTTP API to "White IP" (or "Disabled" if nothing uses it). First check in Analysis › Logs › api who calls it and from which address. This filter compares the address Jeedom retains: it only protects if the X-Forwarded-For headers and remoteip rules pass, and if the “Address diagnosis” (plugin page), opened from a phone on 4G, shows “Retained address whitelisted”: “no”, or “yes” because the retained address really is the phone's (VPN, address added on purpose); “yes” for another address: see the NAT case of the X-Forwarded-For headers rule.

Settings › System › Configuration › API: set the JSON-RPC API to "White IP". Local plugins (Homebridge…) call it from the local network and keep working. This filter compares the address Jeedom retains: it only protects if the X-Forwarded-For headers and remoteip rules pass, and if the “Address diagnosis” (plugin page), opened from a phone on 4G, shows “Retained address whitelisted”: “no”, or “yes” because the retained address really is the phone's (VPN, address added on purpose); “yes” for another address: see the NAT case of the X-Forwarded-For headers rule.

plugins/secaudit/data/checks.json.Jeedom prend l'adresse du client dans de: Jeedom takes the client address from headers anyone can send (CF-Connecting-IP, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, Client-IP). The fix depends on the architecture, to be checked first: open the “Address diagnosis” (plugin page) from a phone on 4G (no Wi-Fi, no VPN; if Jeedom can only be reached through a VPN, through the VPN), through every access address in use (ddns, Jeedom DNS, Cloudflare…), note its values, and compare with the phone's public IP (any “what is my IP” site, same phone, same family IPv4 or IPv6; through a VPN, compare instead with the phone's VPN address, shown in the VPN app). a) Connection address = the phone's IP: direct access. b) Different connection address, and the phone's IP in the address seen by Apache or in a header received: a proxy is on the path, at the connection address (127.0.0.1 for nginx or a tunnel on the Jeedom machine, Jeedom DNS, Tailscale, cloudflared, Cloudflare, remote proxy…), even if you did not install one. c) The phone's IP nowhere (no address or header shown): NAT (VM gateway, Docker, router) or a proxy that does not pass the address on; declare nothing in remoteip (a declared address can choose its clients' address). Address retained by Jeedom = 127.0.0.1, ::1 or an address of the Jeedom machine: a local tunnel or proxy that does not pass the address on; make it pass it (X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP), then run the diagnosis again, and never remove this address from the whitelist (Jeedom's daemons use it). d) Connection address “unknown” (PHP not running as an Apache module, sudo refused to www-data, or ss missing): if the phone's IP appears nowhere, it is c); otherwise neither disable nor declare anything before reading the connection address: over SSH, run `sudo ss -tnp state established` right after reloading the page from the phone, several times, and read only the apache2 or httpd lines whose local address is on an Apache listening port (80, 443…). Before that, close the other apps and other tabs that reach Jeedom (JeedomConnect…) and wait 10 s after any test through another access address. If the phone's IP is only in a header received (not in the address seen by Apache), it is b), whatever ss shows. Otherwise, it is a) only if the phone's IP is, on every reading, the only address of those lines; a 127.0.0.1 or ::1 line during the reload points to a likely local proxy: b), to confirm in its configuration. Another address may be another visitor's: declare it only if the proxy's configuration confirms it (Jeedom DNS: Settings › System › Configuration › Networks), never from ss alone. When in doubt, declare nothing. At every `apache2ctl configtest && …`: if configtest fails, neither reload nor restart Apache; fix until configtest passes, or roll back the step at once. A failing configuration would stop Apache from restarting. The fix must suit every access address: first declare each proxy found in b) (2), run the diagnosis again, then do 1). Otherwise 1) would give every visitor the proxy's address, often whitelisted (127.0.0.1, 10.*, 192.168.*): no more banning. Direct access only (a): do 1), and also fix the remoteip rule if it fails. 1) If /etc/apache2/conf-available/secaudit-entetes.conf already exists, keep a copy for reference (`sudo cp -n /etc/apache2/conf-available/secaudit-entetes.conf /root/`, which does not overwrite a copy already made); create it (or replace its content) with the 4 lines `RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-For "expr=%{REMOTE_ADDR}"`, `RequestHeader unset X-Real-IP`, `RequestHeader unset CF-Connecting-IP`, `RequestHeader unset Client-IP`, without “early” (they must run after remoteip), then `sudo a2enmod headers`, `sudo a2enconf secaudit-entetes`, `sudo apache2ctl configtest && sudo systemctl reload apache2` (if configtest fails, neither reload nor restart Apache: it keeps the old configuration; fix the file until configtest passes, then reload). Remove any old `RequestHeader … early` line if a proxy is declared. 2) Declaring a proxy in remoteip: `sudo cp /etc/apache2/conf-enabled/remoteip.conf /root/remoteip.conf.avant` (Jeedom's file, keep it: Jeedom recreates it if missing), then, inside the `<IfModule mod_remoteip.c>` block, replace the existing RemoteIPHeader line with `RemoteIPHeader <header carrying the phone's IP: the one among the headers received; keep the current one if the address seen by Apache carries it; Forwarded is not read by remoteip: make the proxy send X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP, then run the diagnosis again; until then, change nothing>` and add `RemoteIPInternalProxy <connection address>` (local address, 127.0.0.1 included) or `RemoteIPTrustedProxy <connection address>` (public address), one line per proxy found; for Cloudflare (several ranges), `RemoteIPHeader CF-Connecting-IP` and `RemoteIPTrustedProxyList /etc/apache2/cloudflare-ips.txt`, a file of the ranges published on cloudflare.com/ips (IPv4 and IPv6, one per line, to keep up to date). For the header, prefer the one the declared proxy sets itself (X-Forwarded-For appended, X-Real-IP rewritten), never a header it only relays: a client reaching this proxy without going through the previous one could forge it. Chained proxies (Cloudflare → nginx…): if after declaring, the address retained by Jeedom is another proxy's, declare that one too (Cloudflare: its ranges) and run the diagnosis again. Then `sudo a2enmod remoteip` and `sudo apache2ctl configtest && sudo systemctl reload apache2`. Rollback: `sudo cp /root/remoteip.conf.avant /etc/apache2/conf-enabled/remoteip.conf`, `sudo a2dismod remoteip` if it was disabled before, then `sudo apache2ctl configtest && sudo systemctl reload apache2`. With NAT (c), Apache does not know the visitors' real address: if “whitelisted” is “yes” and the retained address is not the Jeedom machine's (see c)), note the current list (Settings › System › Configuration › Security, for rollback), then replace the entry covering the address retained by Jeedom with narrower entries covering the local machines without it. Beware: every access going through this gateway, local network included (Docker, VM with NAT), loses the whitelist (APIs in White IP mode refused), and a few failed logins by an attacker get it banned: no access through it at all, web interface included, for the ban duration. If local network devices go through this gateway, do not narrow the list. Rollback without the web interface, over SSH (`su -`, then): `php -r 'require_once "/var/www/html/core/php/core.inc.php"; config::save("security::whiteips", "<noted list>"); cache::delete("security::banip");'`. The real fix is a redirect that keeps the source address (network bridge, port forwarding without source NAT) or a proxy that passes the address on. Check, from the phone, through every access address: the address retained by Jeedom must be the phone's public IP (with NAT: the same as before, the gateway's). If it became a local or proxy address while the diagnosis showed the phone's IP before, roll back at once. Rollback of 1): `sudo a2disconf secaudit-entetes` (only removes rules, never cuts access, but also removes an older active version of this file: the audit will report it again; any older version stays in /root for reference); then `sudo apache2ctl configtest && sudo systemctl reload apache2`.
